list.listitem: Suspect cavernous sinus thrombosis in a patient with acute onset of unilateral periorbital swelling, headache, photophobia, chemosis, proptosis, ptosis, and cranial nerve palsies progressing to bilateral involvement (especially within 48 hours). B
Obtain MRI or CT with contrast-enhanced venography to confirm the diagnosis. B
Mainstay of therapy is IV antibiotics and surgical drainage. B
Early recognition and prompt treatment reduces mortality risk. C

background.definition: Cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is a rare entity characterized by infection and formation of blood clots in the cavernous sinus, associated with fever, headache, and progressive orbital and periorbital edema.

list.listitem: Rare; incidence has declined since first half of 20th century with the advent of antibiotics.
A 2018-2019 study published in 2022 estimates that the incidence rates of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis ranges between 2.45 and 3.16 per 100, 000 persons in the US.
There are 3 main types of cavernous sinus thrombosis, septic, aseptic and chronic types

Most cases are the septic form, in which infection precedes and initiates thrombosis of the CST. Usually, there is contiguous spread of infection from adjacent structures or areas with venous drainage to the cavernous sinuses. Such areas include sphenoid, ethmoid, or frontal sinuses. The source may also be from facial, dental, oropharyngeal, middle ear, and orbital infections (orbital cellulitis)

The aseptic form is initiated by thrombosis from prior cavernous sinus surgery, hypercoagulability, pregnancy, oral contraceptive pills, neoplasms, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and trauma. There may be secondary bacterial infection
The chronic form is rare and may occur from dental, sinus, and facial infections, especially of fungal cause
Most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus (60%-70% of cases)
Other bacteria include streptococcal species (second leading cause, 20% of cases), pneumococcal species, Gram-negative rods, and anaerobes.
Fungal infections from aspergillosis and mucormycosis also occur.
Rare causes are coronavirus disease-19 (COVID-19) infection and vaccination .
CST occurs in all ages, though more so in young adults. In immunosuppressed patients, consider fungal etiology.
The cavernous sinuses are a pair of dural sinuses located on either side of the sella turcica and enclosed between the layers of the dura mater.

The cavernous sinuses are related anteriorly to the optic chiasma, medially to the pituitary gland within the sella turcica, laterally to the temporal lobe of the brain, and inferiorly to the sphenoid sinus.

Within the lateral walls of the sinuses are cranial nerves (CN III, IV, and V); the carotid artery and abducens nerve (CN VI) course within the sinuses. Venous supplies from the face, orbits, sinuses, and brain drain into the cavernous sinus. Also, the pair of cavernous sinuses maintains intercavernous connections.

Infections away from the eye precede CST by 5 days to 10 days, during which the microbial agent spreads through the veins to the cavernous sinus. Infective agents within the cavernous sinus initiate the coagulation cascade, with resultant blood clot formation.

COVID-19 infection and its related vaccination may cause CST likely by creating a generalized prothrombotic state . The incidence in patients hospitalized with COVID-19 was 231/1,000,000 person-years; women under age 50 years had the highest incidence.
Clinical findings result from impairment in venous drainage from the orbit and eye and from mechanical pressure on the structures within the sinus or its wall.
Largely a clinical diagnosis with proptosis, chemosis, and ptosis seen in more than 90% of cases. B

MRI or CT scan with contrast-enhanced venography are the preferred diagnostic methods. Findings of asymmetrical enlargement of a sinus with irregular filling defects and engorgement of the superior orbital vein is very suggestive of CST. Diffusion-weighted MRI finding of cavernous sinus hyperintensity supports diagnosis. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Unilateral, no systemic illness, no source of infection external to eye, negative culture

list.listitem: Clinical presentation of fever, ptosis, chemosis, proptosis, and external ophthalmoplegia should prompt a suspicion of CST and lead to initiation of diagnostic workup to confirm the diagnosis.

Findings are initially unilateral but can become bilateral within 24 hours to 48 hours, especially without treatment, as a result of disease spread through the intercavernous sinus connections. Spread of clinical findings to involve the contralateral eye within 24 hours to 48 hours is characteristic of CST.
Symptoms include headache (when present is severe and frontal or retroorbital), fever (picket fence pattern), photophobia, and progressive unilateral then bilateral orbital and periorbital swelling.

Signs include acute swelling of the eyelid, with redness of the eye (conjunctival chemosis) from obstruction of the ophthalmic veins. Subsequently, there is proptosis of the eye. Other signs include cranial nerve palsies. Extraocular motility problems occur often with lateral rectus palsy preceding as the sixth cranial nerve travels within the cavernous sinus. Involvement of the third cranial nerve further compounds the extraocular motility abnormalities and produces ptosis and dilation of the pupil.
Sensory deficits involving facial area supplied by the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the fifth cranial nerve occur often.
Meningismus occurs in about 40% of cases, as well as altered sensorium, tachycardia, and sepsis. Diplopia, seizures, and hemiparesis occur in less than 20% of cases.
Fundoscopy often shows ill-defined disc margins with signs of venous engorgement, including retinal hemorrhages, diminished visual acuity, and blindness.

Often there is peripheral leukocytosis; positive blood cultures confirm underlying systemic infection. Blood cultures are positive in about 70% of patients. Although most patients have abnormal CSF with elevations in WBC counts and protein levels, the CSF culture is positive in only about 20%.
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast-enhanced venography are preferred diagnostic methods.

Imaging with coronal views of the cavernous sinuses is very helpful. The findings in CST include asymmetry of the cavernous sinuses, flattening or bulging of the lateral wall from enlargement of the sinus, irregular filling defects within the enhancing sinus, and engorgement of the superior ophthalmic vein.
Additional findings include hyperintensity of the cavernous sinus and cerebral infarcts on diffusion-weighted MRI, and cavernous internal carotid artery narrowing on CT or MR angiography.
CST may be undetectable by imaging very early in disease.
Consider diagnosis in patient with acute onset of unilateral periorbital swelling, headache, photophobia, chemosis, proptosis, ptosis, and cranial nerve palsies.
Obtain MRI or CT scan with contrast-enhanced venography .

Treatment involves parenteral fluids, antibiotics, and surgical drainage of source infection. Consider antifungal agent if no response to broad-spectrum antibiotics or with negative cultures or in immunosuppressed patients.
Parenteral high-dose antibiotic is recommended. Add an antifungal if fungal etiology suspected. B
Surgical drainage may be indicated for paranasal source of infection, dental abscess, orbital abscess, and complicating subdural empyema. C
Anticoagulation is recommended for selected patients. C
Prescribe high-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms. Antifungals may be added in diabetic or immunosuppressed patients.

Broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage can be obtained with a combination of oxacillin or nafcillin (2 g every 4 hours) added to a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin with activity against pseudomonas (ceftazidime 2 g every 8 hours) or a carbapenem (imipenem 2 g every 6 hours). For anaerobic coverage, metronidazole 500 mg every 6 hours is added.

Vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours, in place of nafcillin, is given if methicilin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is demonstrated. Reports of septic CST caused by community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) in immunocompetent individuals suggest that physicians may consider antibiotics that are active against CA-MRSA when choosing empiric antibiotic coverage for septic CST.
Amphotericin B is the antifungal often used. Posaconazole has also been used in patients with mucormycosis, although clinical trials are lacking.

Duration of therapy may last from 3 to 8 weeks depending on persistence of primary site infection or complicating abscess. In general, treatment is required for at least 2 additional weeks beyond clinical resolution.
Early, aggressive antibiotic treatment is associated with lower morbitdity and mortality. Adjust antibiotics with microbial sensitivity results.

Early anticoagulation, though not widely accepted, with heparin transitioned to warfarin (target INR of 2-3) for 1 to 9 months has been suggested to reduce progression of CST and its complications. Avoid anticoagulation in the presence of venous infarcts, intracranial or orbital hemorrhage, or epistaxis. Otherwise, generally for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, the limited available evidence suggests that anticoagulation is safe and may be effective in reducing adverse outcomes.
Corticosteroids may be used in the setting of meningitis or dysfunction of the adrenal and pituitary glands. Otherwise, their use to reduce morbidity of CST is controversial.
Consider surgical drainage of paranasal source of infection, dental abscess, orbital abscess, and complicating subdural empyema.
It is only recommended for drainage of primary source of infection or other concurrent localized abscess.
Complications include persisting morbidity despite treatment, late sequelae, relapses, and mortality.
Persisting morbidity includes oculomotor palsy (in 17% of cases), blindness (17%), hemiparesis (3%), and pituitary insufficiency (2%).

Other complications that occur from extension of infection and thrombosis to surrounding intracranial or distant structures include subdural empyema, meningitis, cerebral abscess, orbital abscess, other cerebral venous thrombosis, and carotid thrombosis with ischemic strokes. Distant spread of infection results in pneumonia, pneumothorax, lung abscess, and empyema.
Prompt admission and treatment in an intensive care unit are advocated, because CST can be rapidly fatal.
One-third to one-half of patients show persisting sequelae of illness despite treatment. B
Relapses can occur on treatment completion. B
Early recognition and prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotic cover reduce the chance of mortality. B
Long-term anticoagulation may be beneficial.
